answer.rationale: The strongest signal is temporal: a release landed 2h ago and write-path p99 began climbing 90m ago, which fits a post-deploy regression better than pure load (settlement peak is a recurring, presumably provisioned-for event, and memory_b3 says headroom absorbed a comparable surge). Rollback also directly addresses cause rather than symptom, which matters most for sustained availability. I want to verify memory_b1 because it is the only rollback precedent and, as a consolidated summary, it may be hiding the conditions under which rollback was safe — specifically whether it was executed under heavy write load or during a quiet window, and whether 'no customer impact' meant no in-flight writes were dropped. I want memory_b6 because it tells me whether staged/canary gating exists here; if it does, I can roll back one cohort first and confirm latency recovery before going wide, and if canaries did NOT catch this build, that itself is diagnostic about whether the release is really the cause. Note a real competing hypothesis I am not discarding: memory_b5 describes read load on the primary degrading write latency, and route_read_replicas would also fit 'write p99 climbing at peak' — if verification shows b1's rollback happened under low write volume, or shows the current release touched nothing on the write path, I would switch to the replica routing option. Caveat on the inherited record as a whole: all six memories are success stories with no recorded failures or costs, which is a survivorship pattern; they should be read as 'this once worked' rather than 'this reliably works,' and I am weighting them accordingly rather than treating the base rates as established. Scale is deliberately a small guarded rollback: at daily settlement peak the dominant risk is losing in-flight customer writes during a version transition, so I want drain-and-confirm on a limited slice with write-loss instrumentation before committing the full fleet, accepting slower recovery in exchange for not violating the harder constraint.
